readings.title: A warmer reading room
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
An old library had a cold reading room in winter. Staff wanted people to stay and study, but the room seemed empty on some afternoons. The central difficulty was uneven warmth near the large windows. Visitors near the windows wore coats while people beside the radiator said the air was too warm; a single thermometer hid the difference. The organizers knew that a tidy plan in an office might not match what happened in an ordinary week.

The group first tried temperature notes from several desks. Volunteers recorded readings at different hours and asked visitors where they chose to sit, rather than relying on one measurement at the door. They therefore listened to people who used the place at different times, including those who seldom attended formal meetings.

The trial showed the coldest seats were occupied least often. The pattern remained after staff compared weekdays and weekends; low use was linked to comfort rather than a lack of interest in books. In response, the group adopted window seals and a new seating plan. Maintenance workers repaired gaps around two windows, and staff moved quiet-study tables to places with a steadier temperature. The notes did not remove every disagreement, but they made the reasons for the next decision easier to explain.

The broader lesson was clear: comfort must be measured where people actually sit. A building-wide average can conceal an uncomfortable corner, so future checks will include both measurements and visitor experiences. Keeping a record of small changes also helped the team distinguish a temporary setback from a lasting problem. For the people involved in a warmer reading room, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: Sharing electricity from a roof
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A housing cooperative considered solar panels on its common roof. Members liked the idea but had different expectations about the savings. The central difficulty was unclear evening electricity demand. Most residents were at work during sunny hours, and the board did not know how much daytime power shared rooms could use. A first impression was not enough to tell the whole story, because different people approached the service in different ways.

The group first tried a month of shared-meter readings. The cooperative measured electricity used in hallways and a laundry room, then compared the figures with predicted solar output. The team compared comments with direct observations rather than assuming that the loudest opinion represented everyone.

The trial showed the laundry room used most power after sunset. A daytime production estimate alone therefore overstated the benefit; residents also asked how maintenance costs would be divided. In response, the group adopted a smaller solar proposal with clear costs. The board reduced the panel area and circulated a plain-language estimate that included equipment care and possible future replacement. Some suggestions were inexpensive, while others would have required a change to staffing or equipment.

The broader lesson was clear: energy plans need realistic timing and costs. Members could support a modest plan once they understood when power would be produced and who would pay for upkeep. The final proposal remained open to revision when new information became available. For the people involved in sharing electricity from a roof, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: Insulating a row of small homes
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A local advice centre helped households reduce heating bills. It began by offering the same checklist to every home in one street. The central difficulty was different causes of heat loss in similar houses. Some rooms had draughts around doors, while others had poor roof insulation; a standard instruction could waste limited money. Several participants valued the original aim even though they questioned the first method chosen to reach it.

The group first tried short visits by trained advisers. Advisers asked residents which rooms felt cold and examined simple, visible features before suggesting any purchase or building work. Short conversations after the activity revealed details that a written form had failed to capture.

The trial showed door seals helped one home but not another. A neighbour with sound doors needed roof advice instead, showing why the most visible problem is not always the main one. In response, the group adopted house-specific advice and follow-up calls. The centre offered low-cost suggestions first, checked whether they helped after a month, and referred complex problems to qualified specialists. The people responsible made their limits clear and invited others to describe any unintended effects.

The broader lesson was clear: similar buildings can need different solutions. The centre kept its general checklist as a starting point, but decisions now depended on each household’s actual conditions. This approach gave the group a practical basis for its next round of work. For the people involved in insulating a row of small homes, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

readings.title: Lighting a path without waste
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Residents asked for better lighting on a route to the evening bus. The council wanted to improve safety while limiting energy use. The central difficulty was dark sections beside a busy crossing. A map of existing lamps looked complete, yet one bend remained poorly lit because trees blocked the light at pedestrian height. The project began on a small scale so that its organizers could learn before making a permanent commitment.

The group first tried night walks with residents and engineers. The group observed the path at bus arrival times and marked where people slowed down or stepped into the road. They noted both benefits and costs, including the time that volunteers or staff needed to give.

The trial showed one shaded bend mattered more than the whole path. Most of the route was already usable, so installing equally bright lamps everywhere would spend money without addressing the main concern. In response, the group adopted targeted lamps and regular tree checks. Engineers changed two light positions and arranged to inspect branches that could later block the lamps again. The public summary described what had changed and what questions had not yet been answered.

The broader lesson was clear: safety improvements can be focused and efficient. Residents valued the change because it addressed a specific difficulty while keeping the rest of the route modestly lit. Readers could therefore judge the decision by its evidence rather than by a promise of perfect results. For the people involved in lighting a path without waste, the result was useful because it connected an everyday difficulty with a change they could see and discuss. No one claimed that a single trial could settle every question. The group planned to watch what happened over time and to explain any further changes openly.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A public reading room should be judged from the visitor’s point of view. In one library, a thermometer near the door suggested that the building was warm enough. People sitting beside the windows disagreed because cold air reached their desks. Staff recorded temperatures in several places and asked visitors when they chose to stay. They discovered that the least comfortable seats were often empty. Repairing the window seals was a modest step, but it made the room easier to use. The library plans to check the results again during the next winter. A single average figure is helpful only when it does not hide important differences within a space.
translation.explanation: 注意主语视角、because原因关系和only when条件关系。
translation.referenceAnswer: 公共阅览室应从访客的角度来评价。在一家图书馆，门边的温度计显示建筑似乎足够暖和，坐在窗边的人却有不同感受，因为冷空气吹到了他们的桌边。工作人员记录了不同位置的温度，并询问访客何时愿意留下。他们发现最不舒服的座位常常空着。修补窗户密封处虽然只是小改动，却让阅览室更好用。图书馆计划在下一个冬天再次检查效果。单一平均数只有在不掩盖空间内重要差异时才有帮助。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to a library manager proposing a practical way to make the reading room more comfortable in winter. Explain what should be observed, what could be changed first, and how the result should be checked.
writing.explanation: 范文说明观察位置、先期改动与效果复查。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Library Manager,
I would like to suggest a small winter comfort project for the reading room. Several visitors avoid the desks beside the windows, although the temperature near the entrance seems reasonable. Staff could measure the air at different desks during morning and afternoon visits. A short question at the desk would also show which places readers prefer and why.
If the window area is consistently colder, repairing the seals would be a sensible first step. The library could move a few tables while that work is arranged. After the change, please repeat the measurements and ask visitors whether they can study comfortably for longer. Publishing a brief summary would help readers see that their comments have been taken seriously.
Yours sincerely,
A regular visitor
